performers: Arthur Whittemore and Jack Lowe; RCA Victor Symphony Orchestra; Dimitri Mitropoulos
intro: A solo piano begins with a melody in Mozart’s manner; the second piano carries it into Poulenc’s Paris. Arthur Whittemore and Jack Lowe play the concerto’s Larghetto with Dimitri Mitropoulos in a 1947 recording.

sections.label: B · Plus allant: two busy pianos
A′ · The opening tune returns
sections.mNote: Piano melody over plucked strings, then a winding second piano

cues.title: One piano, Mozart’s shadow
cues.text: The first piano plays alone in B♭ major, a singing tune above a gently rocking accompaniment. Poulenc deliberately borrows Mozart’s manner. The second piano answers with a melody of its own before the orchestra joins the conversation.
cues.evidence: Poulenc, full score, Rouart, Lerolle & Cie., plate R.L. 11887, pp. 37–40: solo first piano, then second piano, followed by the orchestra. Steven Ledbetter’s Boston Symphony note quotes Poulenc on the Mozartian opening: https://www.bso.org/works/poulenc-concerto-in-d-minor-for-two-pianos
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two pianos in Venice
cues.text: The Princesse de Polignac commissions the concerto in 1932. At its first performance in Venice that September, Poulenc and Jacques Février sit at the two pianos; Désiré Defauw conducts the orchestra of La Scala.
cues.evidence: Steven Ledbetter, Boston Symphony programme note: commission, summer 1932 composition and première on 5 September 1932, with Poulenc, Février, Defauw and the La Scala orchestra. https://www.bso.org/works/poulenc-concerto-in-d-minor-for-two-pianos

cues.title: Plus allant
cues.text: Poulenc marks the middle section Plus allant — more flowing. Both pianos play short chords, with a tune rising above them. Strings and wind instruments join the exchanges, and the quiet concerto grows into a full orchestral climax.
cues.evidence: Full score, Rouart, Lerolle & Cie., plate R.L. 11887, rehearsal 34 on p. 45 through pp. 54–55: Plus allant and the increasingly forceful orchestral writing. https://petruccimusiclibrary.ca/files/imglnks/caimg/d/d9/IMSLP376787-PMLP489112-Poulenc_-_Concerto_for_Two_Pianos_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mozart returns
cues.text: The opening tune returns in the first piano at the original tempo, supported by plucked strings. The second piano adds a winding line, while wind instruments hold soft chords around the two soloists.
cues.evidence: Full score, Rouart, Lerolle & Cie., plate R.L. 11887, p. 59, Tempo I, and rehearsal 40: the opening first-piano phrase returns over pizzicato strings; piano 2 and sustained wind parts follow. https://petruccimusiclibrary.ca/files/imglnks/caimg/d/d9/IMSLP376787-PMLP489112-Poulenc_-_Concerto_for_Two_Pianos_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clear and quiet
cues.text: The ending pairs the first piano’s held chord with an upward ripple from the second. Poulenc writes clair et p — clear and quiet — over the little run. A short chord ends the movement.
cues.evidence: Full score, Rouart, Lerolle & Cie., plate R.L. 11887, p. 63: piano 1 holds its chord without pedal; piano 2 has rising groups of eight notes marked clair et p, followed by the final short chord. https://petruccimusiclibrary.ca/files/imglnks/caimg/d/d9/IMSLP376787-PMLP489112-Poulenc_-_Concerto_for_Two_Pianos_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Arthur Whittemore (piano), Jack Lowe (piano), RCA Victor Symphony Orchestra (orchestra), Dimitri Mitropoulos (conductor)
fields.note: The original labels and RCA's contemporary advertisement name all four performing credits. The sources consulted do not allocate the first and second piano parts to the individual pianists.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original orchestral scoring; complete second movement
fields.note: The transfer joins the two 78-rpm sides containing the Larghetto. The source identifies the original concerto, not a piano reduction. The exact edition used by the performers is unknown. The section landmarks are provisional passage timings, established from the score and the transfer; they have not been reviewed by ear.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The transfer description gives 15 December 1947. The year is retained here; the exact day has not been checked against a session ledger. The item-level date 1947 is the recording year, not the commercial publication year.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: NBC Studio 3-A, New York City, United States
fields.note: Venue as identified by the transfer description.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The automatic-sequence album contains three 12-inch records. RCA's September 1948 magazine advertises both M-1235 and DM-1235. The Larghetto occupies record 12-0368 in the transferred DM set.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Sides 3–4: 12-0368-A and 12-0368-B; matrices D7-RC-8226 and D7-RC-8227
fields.note: Side and record numbers were read on the labels, which also print the corresponding manual-sequence numbers 12-0364-A/B. Matrix numbers are transcribed from the transfer description; no take suffix or stamper has been established.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Host and collection are identified. The original record producer is RCA; no separate personal transfer-engineer credit has been established.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was uploaded on 3 April 2022. Its digitisation date is not stated.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Uploaded FLAC transfer; Internet Archive VBR MP3 derivative
fields.note: The complete-movement MP3 derives from the uploaded FLAC. Playback equipment, side-join method, equalisation, pitch correction and noise reduction are not documented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Separate composition copyright remains in force in life-plus-70 territories; IMSLP identifies public-domain status in Canada.
fields.note: Poulenc died in 1963. IMSLP explicitly warns that this work remains protected in the EU and probably in the US. The accepted historical-phonogram rule below does not clear the underlying composition; no separate permission or worldwide composition licence has been established.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: commercial publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: RCA's September 1948 magazine advertises M/DM-1235 with performers, format and prices. Under the project's pre-1963 phonogram rule, the former 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. The recording is not offered under a Creative Commons licence; US recording status is not established.

composer.epithet: The pianist who wanted butter in the sauce wrote prayers, love songs and an opera in which a guillotine silences the choir.
facts: Piano with Ricardo Viñes; counterpoint and composition with Charles Koechlin
Georges Auric · Jean Cocteau · Guillaume Apollinaire · Paul Éluard
Pierre Bernac, baritone; Denise Duval, soprano; Poulenc at the piano
Three operas, songs, choral music, ballets, concertos and wind sonatas
composer.background:
Ricardo Viñes taught piano with his feet as well as his hands. When his pupil Francis Poulenc mishandled the pedal, a buttoned boot prodded his shin. Poulenc remembered the lessons with affection: “I owe him everything,” he told Claude Rostand in their radio conversations of 1953–54. Viñes taught him to make a staccato note sing through the pedal and to distinguish sharply between kinds of touch. Poulenc eventually acquired his own kitchen-language remedy for a meagre piano sound: “Put butter in the sauce!”

He was born in Paris on 7 January 1899. His father Émile ran a chemical business; his mother Jenny came from a family of Parisian artisans and began teaching him piano when he was five. She played Mozart and Schubert, Chopin and salon pieces. Poulenc’s affections made room for what he later called “adorable bad music”. His uncle Marcel Royer, known as Papoum, took him to concerts and the theatre. The Ballets Russes supplied Stravinsky; Debussy’s scores became household necessities. “It is my oxygen,” he told Rostand of Debussy’s music.
